source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)

coverage.syllabus: IV.C Administrative Rulemaking — procedural regularity pp. 283–306; assigned in Lubbers Fall 2026
coverage.existingCoverage: Previously imported Chapter 5 pp. 225–283; no overlap in new topics

topics.title: § 5.5.1 — Agency Heads' Personal Responsibility in Rulemaking (pp. 283–284)
topics.description: Rulemaking record consideration, staff synopses, Morgan I and Morgan IV tension, FDA dietary-food deposition problem.

entries.title: APA § 553(c) requires consideration of relevant submissions
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: After considering relevant matter presented during comment period, agency must adopt concise statement of basis and purpose; state 1961 MSAPA requires full consideration of written/oral submissions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency must hear and consider important comments but the director needn't personally read every paper.
entries.legalExplanation: § 553(c) is institutional requirement; head remains responsible for decision while staff can summarize enormous administrative record.
entries.examApplication: Identify what submissions were considered, who reviewed summaries, and whether agency's reasoning responds.
entries.examTrap: Do not mistake physical reading of every submission for legal duty.

entries.title: Staff can summarize rulemaking record for agency heads
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Commissioners may depend on staff-prepared summaries but they must faithfully present material views and counterarguments; systematic distortion/suppression may breach consideration duty.
entries.laymanExplanation: Boss can rely on a briefing, but not a rigged briefing that hides one side.
entries.legalExplanation: National Small Shipments allows synopses unless skew becomes so extensive heads cannot satisfy duty to consider record.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish extensive workload from proof of deliberate biased synopsis.
entries.examTrap: No rule requires head to read all 32,000 pages personally.

entries.title: Morgan I and Morgan IV in rulemaking
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Morgan I requires responsible decisionmaker to understand record sufficiently to exercise personal judgment; Morgan IV normally prevents litigants probing mental process by deposing agency head.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone must actually make informed choice; opposing lawyers usually cannot interrogate them about private thought process.
entries.legalExplanation: Formal rate-setting is Morgan I context, but principle may inform § 553(c) rulemaking. Morgan IV barrier makes direct proof difficult.
entries.examApplication: Analyze extraordinary circumstances for discovery while respecting deliberative privilege.
entries.examTrap: Large record and compressed schedule alone are not proven procedural violation.

entries.title: National Small Shipments Traffic Conference v. ICC (D.C. Cir. 1984)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court permitted staff synopses but warned manipulated summaries could defeat legal consideration.
entries.laymanExplanation: A summary must not systematically conceal one side.
entries.legalExplanation: The issue concerns institutional reasoned consideration, not ritual signatures.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook notes; no excerpted judicial opinion

topics.title: § 5.5.2 — Ex Parte Contacts and Political Influence in Rulemaking (pp. 284–298)
topics.description: Full HBO and Sierra Club readings; formal vs informal ex parte; political accountability and public record; assigned subway-routing hypothetical.

entries.title: Rulemaking record serves public comment, agency deliberation and judicial review
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Docket provides basis for informed public response, agency decision, and court's inspection of why action taken; informal § 553 does not independently specify complete exclusive-record mechanism.
entries.laymanExplanation: The record is the evidence and comments everyone can see; secret factual inputs can undermine review.
entries.legalExplanation: Different organic laws, including CAA § 307(d), can impose a more formal docket and central-relevance tests than default § 553.
entries.examApplication: Identify controlling organic statute before applying disclosure standard.
entries.examTrap: A judicial need for record does not mean every political conversation must be logged.

entries.title: Formal rulemaking: APA §§ 556–557 bars ex parte contacts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Formal rulemaking is subject to restrictions on off-record communications; APA § 557(d) requires disclosure of impermissible contact substance and potential response/remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: A trial-like regulatory hearing has tight no-secret-lobbying rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Distinguish formal 556–557 from informal § 553; communications on merits to deciding officers receive statutory treatment.
entries.examApplication: Classify the proceeding first.
entries.examTrap: Don't automatically import the formal prohibition into ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking.

entries.title: Ordinary informal § 553 rulemaking traditionally permits informal contacts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Absent specific statute/rule, informal notice-and-comment rulemaking does not impose per se ban or comprehensive docket log of every ex parte conversation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency policy-makers can meet with affected interests even outside formal public hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: Attorney General's 1947 manual permitted agency knowledge, files and expertise outside notice record; later debate in Home Box Office and Sierra Club.
entries.examApplication: Ask if legislative policy versus individualized adjudication, and specific docket law.
entries.examTrap: Permissible meetings cannot justify rule with crucial secret data contrary to applicable statute.

entries.title: Home Box Office, Inc. v. FCC, 567 F.2d 9 (D.C. Cir. 1977) — historical strict approach
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Panel adopted broad strict post-NPRM no-private-merits-contact doctrine and immediate docketing of all substantive written/oral ex parte communications. The rule was later curtailed and not the dominant modern default.
entries.laymanExplanation: HBO represents historical judicialized approach to informal rulemaking: post-NPRM interested-party substantive contacts forbidden or fully disclosed.
entries.legalExplanation: Court feared two separate records—public vs insiders—frustrated arbitrary/capricious review and fairness because other parties could not rebut interested factual and expert claims. Allowed ordinary pre-NPRM contacts. Subsequent cases and Sierra Club narrowed strict reading; Vermont Yankee constraints counseled against creating extra procedures.
entries.examApplication: On exam state HBO then explain why Sierra Club rejects its broad application to general informal policymaking.
entries.examTrap: Do not present HBO's blanket ban as governing modern ordinary informal rulemaking.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded assigned textbook
entries.facts: FCC restricted pay cable/sports/movies to safeguard free broadcasters. After public argument, private industry groups held many unequal private meetings with FCC; public-interest intervenors had none. Full substance not placed in public review record.
entries.issue: After NPRM in informal FCC rulemaking, should agency decisionmakers accept private merits communications not disclosed for other commenters and judicial review?
entries.holding: Panel adopted broad strict post-NPRM no-private-merits-contact doctrine and immediate docketing of all substantive written/oral ex parte communications. The rule was later curtailed and not the dominant modern default.
entries.reasoning: Court feared two separate records—public vs insiders—frustrated arbitrary/capricious review and fairness because other parties could not rebut interested factual and expert claims. Allowed ordinary pre-NPRM contacts. Subsequent cases and Sierra Club narrowed strict reading; Vermont Yankee constraints counseled against creating extra procedures.
entries.rule: HBO represents historical judicialized approach to informal rulemaking: post-NPRM interested-party substantive contacts forbidden or fully disclosed.

entries.title: HBO distinctions: before versus after NPRM; substance versus process
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: HBO permitted pre-notice informal lobbying but barred secret substantive post-NPRM merits negotiations among parties and decisionmaker.
entries.laymanExplanation: Early research meetings different from secret lobbying during final public docket.
entries.legalExplanation: HBO worried fact-specific assertions might never face adversarial response, frustrating independent reasoned choice.
entries.examApplication: Date the meetings and describe content.
entries.examTrap: Sierra Club later limited the categorical rule.

entries.title: Sierra Club v. Costle, 657 F.2d 298 (D.C. Cir. 1981) — modern limits on ex parte ban
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: No. CAA and federal § 553 did not categorically prohibit informal policymaking conversations. Material facts/data of central relevance used to support rule must be docketed as statute directs. President's undisclosed policy meeting was permissible where not source of undisclosed essential data. Congressional pressure invalidates only when it targets statutorily irrelevant factors and actually affects decision; not shown.
entries.laymanExplanation: General informal rulemaking permits private/political discussions; record-relevant facts/data may require disclosure under organic statute; pure White House policy contacts not automatically docketed; congressional coercion must involve extraneous statutory factors and affect outcome.
entries.legalExplanation: Policy rulemaking must remain accessible to affected interests and President supervising executive policymaking. Congress chose to bar ex parte in adjudication/formal rulemaking, not general § 553. Court rejected HBO blanket approach and court-added procedural requirements under Vermont Yankee; final rule still must be justified from record. CAA § 307(d)(4)(B)(i) controls central relevance of postcomment oral facts, while executive policy exchanges are treated differently. Congressional political advocacy of constituents allowed unless extraneous and causative.
entries.examApplication: Run four inquiries: governing procedure; substantive versus policy contact; duty to docket central facts; inappropriate Congress influence test.
entries.examTrap: A secret policy conversation with President is not automatically illegal or evidence of improper merits basis; nor is every off-record scientific fact permissible.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded assigned textbook
entries.facts: EPA promulgated new-source sulfur dioxide coal power standard. After comment period coal interests, environmental advocates, Senator Byrd and President Carter/White House officials had meetings. EDF alleged private 'ex parte blitz' caused less restrictive regulation. Clean Air Act § 307(d) required docket for centrally relevant documents/data.
entries.issue: Do undisclosed private, congressional and White House meetings after notice/comment invalidate ordinary informal emissions rulemaking? What disclosure or statutory constraints apply?
entries.holding: No. CAA and federal § 553 did not categorically prohibit informal policymaking conversations. Material facts/data of central relevance used to support rule must be docketed as statute directs. President's undisclosed policy meeting was permissible where not source of undisclosed essential data. Congressional pressure invalidates only when it targets statutorily irrelevant factors and actually affects decision; not shown.
entries.reasoning: Policy rulemaking must remain accessible to affected interests and President supervising executive policymaking. Congress chose to bar ex parte in adjudication/formal rulemaking, not general § 553. Court rejected HBO blanket approach and court-added procedural requirements under Vermont Yankee; final rule still must be justified from record. CAA § 307(d)(4)(B)(i) controls central relevance of postcomment oral facts, while executive policy exchanges are treated differently. Congressional political advocacy of constituents allowed unless extraneous and causative.
entries.rule: General informal rulemaking permits private/political discussions; record-relevant facts/data may require disclosure under organic statute; pure White House policy contacts not automatically docketed; congressional coercion must involve extraneous statutory factors and affect outcome.

entries.title: Sierra Club: CAA central relevance docketing
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: CAA § 307(d) requires all central-relevance documents and, in circumstances, summaries of centrally relevant oral factual/data contacts. Agency has reasonable discretion judging relevance.
entries.laymanExplanation: If hidden meeting brought crucial emissions research, put substance on record; agency needn't transcript every chat.
entries.legalExplanation: Need docket for judicial verification final rule grounded in public evidentiary material, while avoid blanket log rejected in Sierra Club.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether communication transmitted new evidence/data central to justification.
entries.examTrap: This docketing obligation rests on CAA-specific text, not plain § 553 alone.

entries.title: Sierra Club: President/White House policy meetings
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: President may consult executive agency administrators during and after comment period on policy and interagency cost/energy tradeoffs, absent Congress limiting; nondisclosure of meeting acceptable where no essential extra-record data relied on.
entries.laymanExplanation: The President can push an executive agency's general energy policy, not secretly feed unreviewable facts that justify a rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Article II supervisory function and Vermont Yankee caution counsel limited judicial policing of political oversight; only bound by statute and adequate public-record support.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish political view ('rules too costly') from new scientific data omitted from docket.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume same leniency for quasi-adjudication or independent agencies.

entries.title: Sierra Club: congressional pressure two-prong test
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Rule invalid for congressional interference only if pressure designed to force agency to use statutorily irrelevant factors AND agency determination affected by them.
entries.laymanExplanation: Senator advocating coal jobs is allowed if statute permits economics; illegal pressure requires wrong consideration and impact.
entries.legalExplanation: D.C. Federation v Volpe test; senator Byrd's representation of constituents permissible absent substantial evidence of improper SALT trade and causal change.
entries.examApplication: Compare ordinary constituency advocacy with threat tied to treaty vote on irrelevant ground, and prove effect.
entries.examTrap: Mere newspaper allegation of arm-twisting did not suffice in Sierra Club.

entries.title: Sierra Club did not immunize all extra-record data reliance
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: When applicable statute confines rule to public docket evidence, decision must be independently justified by that material even though political pressures may influence choices among lawful options.
entries.laymanExplanation: Political input can influence lawful choice, but agency needs public evidence for chosen emissions standard.
entries.legalExplanation: Court separates the legitimacy of lobbying from legal review of factual foundation and agency's stated reasons.
entries.examApplication: Look for undisclosed factual basis, not mere meeting count.
entries.examTrap: Neither CAA nor APA grants unlimited freedom from record-based review.

entries.title: Policy debate: two records versus democratic accessibility
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: HBO favors transparent adversarial fact-checking; Sierra Club and Scalia stress bargaining and representative pressure; Robinson notes both useful dialogue and risk of anecdotal capture.
entries.laymanExplanation: Private conversations can reveal nuance but also give a powerful lobbyist an unfair secret advantage.
entries.legalExplanation: Distinguish empirical/public participation concerns from legal standards; commentary does not override case holdings.

entries.title: Scalia's political model and Robinson's response
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Scalia: agencies need negotiation with industry, NGOs and Congress. Robinson: helps overcome staff capture and clarify priorities but may let anecdote outweigh written evidence and hide tradeoffs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Democratic compromise versus rule-of-law transparency.
entries.legalExplanation: These are views in casebook Notes, not controlling rules.

entries.title: Sangamon Valley Television Corp. v. United States (D.C. Cir. 1959)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Despite formal label as rulemaking, scarce TV frequency effectively allocated between two broadcasters; undisclosed meetings and gifts tainted competitive adjudicative allocation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Choosing between two applicants for one valuable channel is more like a private hearing than general policy.
entries.legalExplanation: Sierra Club recognized possible quasi-adjudicative exception; continued validity after Vermont Yankee debated.
entries.examApplication: Identify competing private claims to fixed scarce privilege.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically call all limited-beneficiary regulations adjudications.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook notes; no excerpted judicial opinion

entries.title: No universal duty to docket under plain § 553; agencies may voluntarily adopt
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Outside special law, no Sierra Club universal oral contact docket duty for ordinary § 553; agencies sometimes independently require contact logs; ACUS 2014–4 recommended full substantive post-NPRM logging.
entries.laymanExplanation: EPA may log significant facts even though ordinary statutory minimum is less.
entries.legalExplanation: Distinguish optional agency transparency rule, binding organic law, and nonbinding ACUS recommendation.
entries.examApplication: Apply state specific rules or internal agency practices to problem.
entries.examTrap: Nonbinding recommendation cannot itself invalidate rule.

entries.title: ACUS and OIRA White House communications policy
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ACUS 80–6 favored undisclosed interagency policy consultations but disclosure of material factual inputs; ACUS 88–9 proposed publication of official written OIRA policy guidance (not every oral contact).
entries.laymanExplanation: Internal policy ideas can be private; crucial factual material should be visible.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasting transparency dissent and executive supervision account; policy recommendations not universal legal commands.

topics.title: § 5.5.3 — Bias and Prejudgment in Rulemaking (pp. 298–306)
topics.description: Full ANA opinion, Cinderella comparison, legislative vs adjudicative facts, Mahoney, Northwestern Bell pipeline hypothetical.

entries.title: Bias standard in rulemaking generally more permissive than adjudication
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: In policy rulemaking, official usually may express regulatory opinions publicly; to disqualify require clear and convincing evidence of unalterably closed mind on critical matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rulemaker may think advertising to children is harmful, as long as they're willing to genuinely consider opposing evidence.
entries.legalExplanation: Association of National Advertisers rejected applying Cinderella's disinterested-observer prejudgment test designed for case-specific adjudication.
entries.examApplication: Classify agency action as rulemaking versus adjudication first.
entries.examTrap: A firm policy position is not itself proof of unalterably closed mind.

entries.title: Association of National Advertisers, Inc. v. FTC (ANA), 627 F.2d 1151 (D.C. Cir. 1979)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: No. Legislative policy rulemaking demands political engagement and prediction. Disqualification only with clear and convincing evidence commissioner has an unalterably closed mind on critical issues; Pertschuk's statements lacked that showing. Court reversed disqualification.
entries.laymanExplanation: For § 18 rulemaking: clear and convincing evidence of unalterably closed mind on matter critical to rule; ideological and expert positions alone permissible.
entries.legalExplanation: FTC § 18 hybrid procedures do not convert rulemaking to adjudication. Adjudication concerns parties' particular past facts; legislative facts in rulemaking are broad empirical assumptions and future risks. Commissioners must arrive with preliminary policy views and remain free to revise based on public comment. Leventhal concurrence endorsed role distinction. MacKinnon dissent would use lower preponderance/substantial-bias test.
entries.examApplication: Compare quotations to respondent-specific prejudgment in Cinderella; ask evidence of refusal to reconsider and stage.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply ordinary adjudicative 'disinterested observer' test mechanically to general rulemaking, or treat any harsh speech as categorical bias.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded assigned textbook
entries.facts: FTC proposed § 18 children's TV advertising restrictions. Chairman Pertschuk repeatedly criticized child exploitation and sugared-food advertising in speeches, interviews and letters before rule. Industry sought recusal; district court applied Cinderella adjudicative bias standard.
entries.issue: Does a rulemaking Commissioner's vigorous prior public advocacy for contemplated advertising regulation require recusal under Cinderella?
entries.holding: No. Legislative policy rulemaking demands political engagement and prediction. Disqualification only with clear and convincing evidence commissioner has an unalterably closed mind on critical issues; Pertschuk's statements lacked that showing. Court reversed disqualification.
entries.reasoning: FTC § 18 hybrid procedures do not convert rulemaking to adjudication. Adjudication concerns parties' particular past facts; legislative facts in rulemaking are broad empirical assumptions and future risks. Commissioners must arrive with preliminary policy views and remain free to revise based on public comment. Leventhal concurrence endorsed role distinction. MacKinnon dissent would use lower preponderance/substantial-bias test.
entries.rule: For § 18 rulemaking: clear and convincing evidence of unalterably closed mind on matter critical to rule; ideological and expert positions alone permissible.

entries.title: ANA standard: clear and convincing unalterably closed mind
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Burden demands persuasive proof of irrevocable predetermined view; normal agency predisposition toward statutory mission is valid.
entries.laymanExplanation: Having a strong view is fine; refusing to hear anything against it is not.
entries.legalExplanation: Presumption of regularity plus pragmatic need for policy debates; narrow disqualification rule.
entries.examApplication: Look for official statement 'no evidence could change my mind' versus passionate advocacy.
entries.examTrap: Judicial standards for hybrid rulemaking and ordinary § 553 may be argued under Vermont Yankee.

entries.title: Legislative facts versus adjudicative facts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: General predictions/risks across regulated industry are legislative facts; determination what one person did at a particular time is adjudicative fact.
entries.laymanExplanation: 'Sugar ads may harm kids' is general policy fact; 'Cinderella lied in its ad' is particular case fact.
entries.legalExplanation: ANA distinguished rulemaking from Cinderella even though hybrid rulemaking allowed cross-examination and substantial evidence review.
entries.examApplication: Name kind of fact and whether disputed fact binds particular litigant.
entries.examTrap: Hybrid process cannot be relabeled quasi-adjudication merely because it contains procedural extras.

entries.title: Public policy discussion is part of agency's job
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Rulemakers must discuss whether government should act and articulate preliminary reasoning in NPRM; they need not start with judicial blank mind.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency wouldn't propose a rule at all if every commissioner had to be neutral on whether the problem exists.
entries.legalExplanation: ANA majority and Leventhal concurrence contrasted judicial role of adjudicator.
entries.examApplication: Assess statutory mission and whether process still genuinely open to comment.
entries.examTrap: Do not make elected or politically accountable officials unable to perform policy functions.

entries.title: MacKinnon dissent to ANA
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Dissent criticized practically impossible closed-mind proof and preferred preponderance evidence of substantial bias, emphasizing special hybrid trial-type protections and individual commissioner advocacy.
entries.laymanExplanation: A strongly biased rulemaker may look incapable of fair listening even without express 'never change' quote.
entries.legalExplanation: This is dissenting perspective, not test adopted by panel.

entries.title: Mahoney v. Shinpoch, 732 P.2d 510 (Wash. 1987)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Washington DSHS unqualified letter committed to reduce public assistance before scheduled public rulemaking hearing; state court invalidated rule for failure to consider comment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not just a strong viewpoint: agency acted as though already finalized before hearing.
entries.legalExplanation: State APA substantive obligation to consider comments; distinguish official predisposition under ANA.
entries.examApplication: Look for official irrevocable action with no conditional language.
entries.sourceRole: Discussed in casebook notes; no excerpted judicial opinion

entries.title: Rulemaking fixed decision before comment can breach procedural duty
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency must actually consider public comments before final rule; objective advance final commitment may violate state APA despite permissive policy bias standard.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency cannot merely hold a pretend hearing after it already sent final instructions.
entries.legalExplanation: Mahoney's unconditional letter to SSA ahead of state hearing showed actual decision; rule invalid absent substantial compliance.
entries.examApplication: Separate judicial recusal against an official from validity of procedural rulemaking itself.
entries.examTrap: ANA permits advocacy, not sham opportunity for comments.

entries.title: Cinderella adjudication vs ANA rulemaking exam contrast
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Adjudication demands neutral factfinder about specific party's allegations; rulemaking expects policy advocate open to changed mind about future class rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Cinderella commissioner said specific school's ads were fraud; ANA chair said industry ads harmful generally.
entries.legalExplanation: Use proceeding's function, adjudicative/legislative facts, standard of proof and appropriate remedy.
entries.examApplication: Write two-column compare and choose correct rule before analysis.
entries.examTrap: One regulation may affect few parties, but that fact alone not convert type.

problems.title: FDA Commissioner / National Nutritional Foods — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 284)
problems.prompt: New FDA Commissioner adopted lengthy dietary food standards 13 days after taking office while signing many other rules. Record included 1,000 pages of exceptions, 20,000 letters, 32,000 testimony pages and exhibits. Manufacturers request Commissioner deposition to test personal consideration. Analyze staff synopses, Morgan I/IV, APA § 553(c) and unusual discovery threshold. Leave result unanswered.

problems.title: HBO v Sierra Club — competing models
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 285–296)
problems.prompt: Compare unequal hidden pay-cable lobbying and general emissions policy outreach. What does judicial review require to protect record accuracy, fairness, and political accountability?

problems.title: Scalia and Robinson debate on private contacts
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 293–295)
problems.prompt: Should ex parte rulemaking discussions be open to negotiation for compromise or docketed to prevent unequal access and anecdotal evidence? Evaluate both without answering.

problems.title: Sangamon scarce-spectrum allocation
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 295–296)
problems.prompt: Does channel allocation between two existing firms warrant adjudication-like restrictions notwithstanding rulemaking format? Reconcile with Vermont Yankee and Sierra Club.

problems.title: Congress and executive branch contact logging
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 296–298)
problems.prompt: When must a Senator, OIRA staff or President disclose policy vs central factual comments? Distinguish the CAA-specific standard from plain § 553 and ACUS voluntary transparency suggestions.

problems.title: Madison Subway / Fillmore University vs Tyler Corp. — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 298)
problems.prompt: MTD chose west-side subway route next to Tyler over east side benefiting Fillmore University after general NPRM. Tyler lobbyists after comment period revealed previously undisclosed expansion plans in private meetings. No statute/agency rule barred or required logging of oral contacts. Assess challenge under HBO, Sierra Club, quasi-adjudicative exceptional circumstances, record fairness and statutory relevance—leave merits unsolved.

problems.title: ANA v Cinderella standards
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 298–305)
problems.prompt: FTC commissioner condemns sugared-food ads before NPRM; separate case targets Kellogg by enforcement complaint without alleging factual distinction among cereal advertisers. Would adjudicative test differ? Analyze parties' specific facts, policy and procedure.

problems.title: ANA standard and Vermont Yankee
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 304–305)
problems.prompt: Is importing judicial unalterably-closed-mind rule to ordinary § 553 consistent with Vermont Yankee? Distinguish constitutional due process, enabling statute and court-added procedure.

problems.title: Mahoney pre-hearing commitment
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 305)
problems.prompt: A welfare agency tells SSA unconditionally that it 'is opting' to cut state benefits three weeks before rulemaking comment hearing. Is this unlawful advance finalization or permissible policy advocacy under ANA? Analyze separately.

problems.title: Sludge Pipeline / Henry MPUC — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 283–306 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 305–306)
problems.prompt: Elected MPUC Commissioner Henry denounced pipeline deregulation and Sludge as lying jackals and planned rip-off. Trial judge barred him from current and all future deregulatory rulemakings. Discuss whether statements show an unalterably closed mind, whether case-specific hostility matters and limits on prospective disqualification—without solving.
